title: Assembly of Gondwana
summary: Gondwana, the great southern supercontinent, was welded together as collisions raised mountain belts across the southern continents, mostly between about 650 and 500 million years ago. They include the East African orogen, the Saharides of North Africa and Arabia, which culminated in the final collision of east and west Gondwana, and the Kuunga orogen, now hidden beneath East Antarctic ice. Rapid erosion of these ranges has been linked to changes in ocean chemistry, more atmospheric oxygen, the rise of animals and the Cambrian explosion.

uncertainty.note: Daczko et al. (2018): numerous 650-500 Ma Gondwana-forming orogens, with Ediacaran-Cambrian (550-500 Ma) amalgamation; Sengor (2020): the Saharides formed from about 900 to 500 Ma, culminating in the final collision.

as_recorded.value: The southern continents preserve numerous 650–500 Ma orogens

when.display: c. 650–500 million years ago (final assembly c. 550–500 Ma)

where.modern_name: Prydz Bay, East Antarctica (suture zone of the Kuunga orogeny linking Indo-Antarctica and Australo-Antarctica; assembly spans Africa, South America, Antarctica, India and Australia)
where.historical_name: Kuunga and East African collisional orogenic belts, Gondwana (no human geography)

paleo.not_applicable: Predates standard plate model reconstructions (older than 500 Ma).

importance.justification: Assembled the southern supercontinent whose mountain building is linked to the oxygen rise and the Cambrian explosion (R4 D3 T4 L2).

beats.caption: Crustal blocks across Africa, South America, Antarctica, and India collided in major orogenic belts around 550 Ma.
Widespread erosion of the Gondwana orogens delivered massive nutrients and oxygen to oceans, fostering early animal radiation.
